questions.q: What does a fixed mindset lead people to do after failure?
a: Give up because they believe their abilities cannot change
Work harder to prove other people wrong
Ask mentors for detailed feedback
Set smaller goals for the next attempt
questions.why: The first lesson says people with a fixed outlook think they cannot change and so stop trying after a setback.

questions.q: What did the Gallup research find about people who use their strengths daily?
a: They were far more engaged and reported a better quality of life
They earned more money but felt less satisfied at work
They changed jobs more often than their peers
They preferred to work alone rather than in teams
questions.why: The second lesson says daily strength use brought six times higher engagement and three times better quality of life.

questions.q: How does the author suggest discovering your strengths?
a: Take online quizzes and ask people who know you well
Copy the skills of the most successful people you know
Spend most of your time fixing your weakest areas
Keep a journal recording your daily mistakes
questions.why: She recommends searching for strength quizzes and asking those closest to you what they think you are good at.

questions.q: Why does the author say your first steps should be tiny?
a: Small steps build consistency and prevent overwhelm
Small goals require much less planning
Small steps make a stronger impression on others
Small steps remove the need for deadlines
questions.why: The third lesson says keeping initial steps almost ridiculously small makes consistency and confidence easier.

questions.q: What does the jar exercise ask you to do?
a: Donate a dollar each time you use negative language
Save a dollar for every goal you complete
Write a compliment and drop it in the jar
Draw one goal from the jar each morning
questions.why: The first lesson suggests putting a dollar in a jar whenever you say I can't, then donating the money to charity.
